report.source_text: The patient was then treated with 0.4 g/kg intravenous immunoglobulin for 10 days, following which partial improvement of the ataxia was detected by a SARA score of 20/40 (gait: 4; stance: 2; sitting: 2; speech disturbance: 3; finger chase: 2; nose-finger test: 2; fast alternating hand movement: 2; heel-shin slide: 3). The patient was then referred to the Department of Medical Oncology, and radioactive iodine treatment was started by nuclear medicine during follow-up. When permanent hypothyroidism occurred, thyroid replacement therapy was also started. The patient’s SARA score was still 20/40 after 6 months of follow-up.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 46-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of gait disorder and poor balance, accompanied by horizontal nystagmus, intention tremor, and ataxic gait. Cerebral MRI revealed significant bilateral cerebellar atrophy. Initial workup showed elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin levels. Malignancy screening identified a suspicious thyroid nodule via ultrasonography and PET/CT. A biopsy indicated suspected papillary carcinoma, which was definitively confirmed as Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC) after bilateral total thyroidectomy. Following the diagnosis of PTC, the patient received intravenous immunoglobulin, resulting in partial improvement of ataxia (SARA score 20/40), which remained stable after 6 months of follow-up, including radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid replacement therapy. The diagnosis of 'definite' PNS was made based on the classical cerebellar syndrome and the presence of cancer developing within 5 years of neurological onset, with onconeural antibodies not being a required criterion.

Cerebral MRI showed significant bilateral cerebellar atrophy in the superior vermis.
An underlying malignancy, Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC), was identified and confirmed.
The cancer developed within 5 years of the neurological disorder onset (2 years of symptoms prior to cancer diagnosis).
Neurological symptoms showed partial improvement with treatment (IVIG) after cancer diagnosis.
